title: Speed and velocity: how fast and which way
summary: Speed divides total distance by total time; velocity divides displacement by total time. See how stops and reversals pull them apart on a position–time graph.

d1.label: $d_1$
d1.body: Covered in [t1:$t_1 = 30\text{ s}$] along the $+x$ direction (moving speed $180/30 = 6\text{ m/s}$).

t1.label: $t_1$
t1.body: Duration of the first moving segment.

t_stop.label: $t_{\text{stop}}$
t_stop.meaning: time paused at the traffic light: 10 s
t_stop.body: Distance covered is zero, yet the clock keeps running—so {total_time|total time} **must** include it.

d2.label: $d_2$
d2.body: Covered in [t2:$t_2 = 10\text{ s}$] along $-x$ (moving speed $60/10 = 6\text{ m/s}$, velocity $-6\text{ m/s}$).

t_total.label: $T$
t_total.meaning: total elapsed time of the whole trip: 50 s
t_total.body: From {total_time|total time}: $T = t_1 + t_{\text{stop}} + t_2 = 30 + 10 + 10 = 50\text{ s}$.

dist.label: $d$
dist.body: From {dist_disp|distance and displacement}: add every leg ($180 + 60 = 240\text{ m}$).

disp.label: $\Delta x$
disp.meaning: net displacement along the road: +120 m (east)

avg_v.label: $v_{\text{av}}$
avg_v.meaning: average speed for the whole trip (scalar), in m/s
avg_v.body: Defined by {avg_speed|average speed} and {speed_vel|speed and velocity}: total [dist:distance] divided by [t_total:total time].

avg_vel.label: $\vec{v}_{\text{av}}$
avg_vel.meaning: average velocity for the whole trip (vector), in m/s with direction
avg_vel.body: Defined by {speed_vel|speed and velocity}: net [disp:displacement] divided by [t_total:total time]. Its direction matches $\Delta\vec{x}$.

unit_conv.title: Converting km/h and m/s
unit_conv.body: Since $1\text{ km} = 1000\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ h} = 3600\text{ s}$, we have $1\text{ m/s} = 3.6\text{ km/h}$. Divide $\text{km/h}$ by $3.6$ (or multiply by $\frac{5}{18}$) to get $\text{m/s}$; multiply $\text{m/s}$ by $3.6$ to get $\text{km/h}$.
unit_conv.useWhen: a problem mixes kilometers per hour with seconds or meters.

inst_vs_avg.title: Average vs. instantaneous velocity
inst_vs_avg.body: **Average velocity** covers a whole time interval $\Delta t$ and equals the slope of the straight secant line connecting start and end on an $x\text{–}t$ graph. **Instantaneous velocity** is the velocity at one exact instant (slope of the tangent line); its magnitude equals instantaneous speed.
inst_vs_avg.analogy: Average speed is your whole-trip summary; instantaneous speed is the number on the speedometer right now.

sections.title: Why speed and velocity disagree
sections.body: In everyday speech, *speed* and *velocity* sound interchangeable. In physics, {speed_vel|speed and velocity} measure two different ratios built from {dist_disp|distance and displacement}. [avg_v:Average speed] asks how much **path** you covered per second, while [avg_vel:average velocity] asks how fast your **position** shifted—and in which direction. Whenever you pause or turn back, the two numbers split apart.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
A student bicycles along a straight east–west road: first [d1:$180\text{ m}$ east] in [t1:$30\text{ s}$], then pauses for [t_stop:$10\text{ s}$] at a red traffic light, and finally turns around to ride [d2:$60\text{ m}$ west] in [t2:$10\text{ s}$].

Taking east as positive, find the [avg_v:average speed] and [avg_vel:average velocity] for the entire trip.

sections.title: List every segment and hidden given
sections.note: notice that both moving legs happen to have the exact same speed ($6\text{ m/s}$)

rows.note: $0\text{ m}$ moved, but still counts in {total_time|total time}
whole trip, including the red-light wait

sections.title: Concept → Field
sections.concept: Divide [dist:total distance] by [t_total:total time] for {avg_speed|average speed}, and divide [disp:net displacement] by the same [t_total:total time] for {speed_vel|average velocity}.
sections.field: Kinematics (1D motion and graphs). Depends on {dist_disp|distance and displacement} and {total_time|total time}.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: why averaging $6\text{ m/s}$ and $6\text{ m/s}$ fails here

routes.title: Route A
routes.why: Going directly from total distance, net displacement, and total elapsed time handles both the pause and the reversal cleanly.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. Always start from the definitions.

routes.title: Route B
routes.path: average the two moving speeds: $(6 + 6)/2 = 6\text{ m/s}$
routes.why: Both moving legs are $6\text{ m/s}$, so $6\text{ m/s}$ looks irresistible.
routes.whyNot: It ignores the [t_stop:$10\text{ s}$ red-light stop] (pulling average speed down to $4.8\text{ m/s}$) and ignores the westward reversal (pulling average velocity down to $+2.4\text{ m/s}$).

sections.notUsed: Not used: {unit_conv|km/h conversion}. Every given is already in SI units ($\text{m}$ and $\text{s}$).

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover a step to check its reason and trap

steps.move: Sum all three intervals to get [t_total:total time].
steps.why: {total_time|Total time} counts the entire clock span from start to finish, stops included.
steps.whyNot: Do not use $30 + 10 = 40\text{ s}$: leaving out the red light gives $6\text{ m/s}$, which is only the moving speed.

steps.move: Find total [dist:distance] and divide by [t_total:$T$] for [avg_v:average speed].
steps.why: {avg_speed|Average speed} uses total path length over total time.
steps.whyNot: Do not subtract $60\text{ m}$ when finding distance; the bicycle wheels rolled forward all $240\text{ m}$.

steps.why: Riding west cancels $60\text{ m}$ of the eastward progress, leaving the student $120\text{ m}$ east of start.
steps.whyNot: Do not drop the sign: if the westward leg were longer than $180\text{ m}$, $\Delta x$ would turn negative.

steps.why: {speed_vel|Average velocity} is displacement per unit total time and points in the direction of $\Delta\vec{x}$ (east).
steps.whyNot: Do not divide by $40\text{ s}$ or omit the direction: average velocity needs both magnitude ($2.4\text{ m/s}$) and direction (east).

sections.title: Position–time graph: slope is velocity
sections.note: drag the eastward distance, return distance, and red-light pause; the straight line's slope is average velocity

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Magnitude rule**: $|\vec{v}_{\text{av}}| = 2.4\text{ m/s} \le 4.8\text{ m/s} = v_{\text{av}}$, because $|\Delta\vec{x}| \le d$ over the same time $T$.
**Zero average velocity**: drag $d_2$ up to $180\text{ m}$ in the plot—the student returns to $x = 0$, so $v_{\text{av},x} = 0\text{ m/s}$ even while $v_{\text{av}} = 7.2\text{ m/s}$.
**Negative velocity**: drag $d_2$ to $240\text{ m}$—the secant slopes downward ($v_{\text{av},x} = -1.2\text{ m/s}$), meaning net motion is **westward**, not "slowing down."
**{unit_conv|Unit sense}**: $4.8\text{ m/s} \times 3.6 = 17.28\text{ km/h}$—a realistic city cycling pace.

questions.q: A car cruises at $72\text{ km/h}$. What is this speed in $\text{m/s}$?
A swimmer swims $50\text{ m}$ to the far wall of a pool and $50\text{ m}$ back to the start in $40\text{ s}$. What are the average speed and average velocity?
questions.why: Total distance is $100\text{ m}$, so $v_{\text{av}} = 100/40 = 2.5\text{ m/s}$. Net displacement is $0\text{ m}$, so $\vec{v}_{\text{av}} = 0\text{ m/s}$.

questions.q: A car drives straight for $60\text{ km}$ at $30\text{ km/h}$ and then another $60\text{ km}$ at $60\text{ km/h}$. What is its average speed for the $120\text{ km}$ trip?
questions.why: The two times are $60/30 = 2\text{ h}$ and $60/60 = 1\text{ h}$, giving $T = 3\text{ h}$ and $v_{\text{av}} = 120/3 = 40\text{ km/h}$ (not the plain mean $45\text{ km/h}$, because more time is spent going slow).

questions.q: On a position–time ($x\text{–}t$) graph, what does a straight line with a **negative slope** mean?
options: The object is moving in the negative direction at constant velocity
The object is slowing down toward a stop
The object's total distance traveled is decreasing
questions.why: On an $x\text{–}t$ graph, slope is {inst_vs_avg|velocity}. A constant negative slope means steady velocity in the $-x$ direction, while distance always increases.
